Ranging from the Qing dynasty to the mid- 20th century, UMAG's silk textile collection encompasses a variety of subjects that fit within the 3x3 account, including hanging scrolls, framed panels, banners and robes. Inspired by famous paintings and works of calligraphy, Mandarin Ducks and Peach Blossoms (Plate 14) is a reproduction of a Song dynasty painting in silk tapestry, while the embroidered calligraphy panel (Fig. 18) vividly illustrates a couple written by Qing dynasty official Weng Tongbo (1840- 1904). Dioxin figures featuring auspicious symbols, such as the Hehe Immortals (Plate 2) and Shoulao, the God of Longevity (Plate 19), are also commonly found throughout the UMAG collection. 
Roughly one quarter of the objects illustrate languid scenes of birds and flowers (Plate 8), while several artworks represent serene landscapes (Plate 1) and figures at leisure. (Plate 17) 
The widespread popularity of silk tapestry and a demand for life- like images resulted in the development of new weaving techniques in the Qing dynasty. As silk tapestry table screens, panels and fans were commonly used as display objects, weavers developed shinagamin toke (double- sided tricot screen silk tapestry) as a way to create a highly ornamented object with identical images on both sides. (Plate 3; Plate 4) Another notable technique known as hekuaixin (mixed- colour threads) combines two or more strands of polychrome threads with similarly coloured areas to produce variations in texture and shades of colour. (Plate 11) For example, the anetrin (three colour gold) technique uses three types of twisted gold and silver threads to achieve a highly expressive pattern. (Plate 7) 
Influenced by the aesthetics of Western painting, Chinese silk tapestry weavers in the mid- and late Qing dynasty began to produce three- dimensional woven works through the use of techniques such as sannan kei (three shades of blue silk tapestry) and shinone kei (water and ink silk tapestry). The former technique employs three different blue threads, including dark blue, reddish blue and pale blue to achieve the various shades; the latter utilizes black, dark grey and light grey with gold or white threads to outline the depicted image. 
Qing dynasty weavers also creatively combined silk tapestry works with other materials or mediums to enhance the quality of woven textiles. Wall hangings and table screens in the imperial palace in the mid- Qing period were often made using the kei mao (silk tapestry with wool) technique, in which the background pattern was woven in silk and the main pattern in wool. For small- area arts that particularly difficult to weave, artisans used brushes to paint in the details; this technique is known as kehua (silk tapestry and painting). (Fig. 12) Another distinctive technique, kezhu (silk tapestry with embroidery), gives finished textiles a shimmering surface, as the fabric ground and specific patterns are first woven into the silk tapestry, and then the remaining motifs are embroidered.
